title: Python
meta: This is a trigger file, not study material. Question visible → answer OUT LOUD → then expand → grade what you missed.
Bullets are keywords and flows, not explanations. If you need the explanation, you're in the wrong file — go to the note.
⭐ = the ones that decide the round. 🔥 = trending 2026. 📍 = you were actually asked this.

Trend-scanned: Aug 2026 · Depth: 03-python/ · Phrasing drill: ⚠️ none — JBTIQ_PY.md retired 24 Aug 2026 (was a duplicate recall grid, not a drill); a real jbtiq_python.md is an open gap · Bank: [[POPULAR-QUESTIONS]] · Scan: [[TREND-SCAN-2026-08]]

questions.text: What does the GIL actually protect, and when does it stop mattering?
points: Protects interpreter state — refcounts, object headers — not your data
One thread executes bytecode at a time; released around I/O and in C extensions
So: I/O-bound threads scale fine · CPU-bound Python threads don't
NumPy / tokenizers / DB drivers drop it → "Python is slow" often isn't the GIL
Your locks are still needed — GIL ≠ thread safety for compound ops
questions.flow: protects interpreter internals → released on I/O and in C → CPU-bound is the only real victim
questions.trap: "the GIL makes Python single-threaded"

questions.text: Threads, processes, or asyncio — how do you pick?
points: Ask one question first: where does the time actually go?
Waiting on network/disk → asyncio (thousands of sockets, one thread)
Waiting, but library is sync-only → threads (bounded pool)
Burning CPU in Python bytecode → processes
Burning CPU in C (NumPy/torch) → threads are fine, GIL is already released
questions.flow: profile first → I/O async · sync-lib threads · Python-CPU processes · C-CPU threads
questions.trap: answering by taste instead of by where the time goes

questions.text: Why is a mutable default argument a bug?
points: Default evaluated once at function definition, not per call
The list/dict is then shared state across every call
Classic tell: accumulating results, "why is my cache global"
Fix: None sentinel → build inside the body
Same root cause as class-attribute-as-mutable
questions.flow: default bound once at def-time → shared object → use None sentinel
questions.trap: describing the symptom without naming def-time evaluation

questions.text: is vs == — and why does is sometimes look right?
points: == → __eq__, value · is → identity, same object
Small ints (−5…256) and some strings are interned → is accidentally passes
Interning is an implementation detail — never a contract
Legit is uses: None, sentinels, enum members
== on floats has its own trap (use tolerance)
questions.flow: value vs identity → interning makes is a liar → is only for singletons
questions.trap: "is is the faster =="

questions.text: Why do generators matter once data gets big?
points: Lazy — produce on demand, constant memory regardless of length
Enables pipelines: read → parse → filter → embed, nothing materialised
Directly relevant to document ingestion and batch embedding
Cost: single-pass, no len(), harder to debug/retry mid-stream
yield from delegates; generators are also the coroutine ancestor
questions.flow: lazy pull → constant memory → chainable pipeline → but single-pass
questions.trap: claiming "faster" — it's memory, not speed

questions.text: Type hints — what do they actually do at runtime?
points: Nothing, by default — CPython does not enforce them
Value is tooling: mypy/pyright, IDEs, refactor safety
Runtime enforcement only where something reads them — Pydantic, FastAPI, dataclasses
That reading is exactly how LLM tool schemas get generated
from __future__ import annotations → strings, changes introspection
questions.flow: ignored at runtime → static tooling → unless a library introspects them
questions.trap: believing annotations validate anything on their own

questions.text: How does async/await actually work under the hood?
points: Coroutine = resumable function; await yields control to the loop
Single-threaded event loop — selector polls ready FDs, resumes callbacks
No preemption: a coroutine runs until it awaits — cooperative
Concurrency ≠ parallelism; one core, interleaved waits
await on something not awaitable-and-yielding = no concurrency gained
questions.flow: coroutine suspends at await → loop polls readiness → resumes → cooperative, single thread
questions.trap: describing it as "runs in the background"

questions.text: What's inside a dict, and why is it ordered now?
points: Compact dict: sparse index array → dense entries array
Dense array is append-order → insertion order is a side effect made official (3.7+)
Open addressing + probing; collisions resolved by probe sequence
Resize on load factor → rehash, order preserved
Key must be hashable and __hash__/__eq__ must agree
questions.flow: sparse indices → dense entries → append order → ordering is structural
questions.trap: saying it's a plain hash table with an added ordered list

questions.text: How does Python free memory?
points: Primary: reference counting — freed the instant count hits zero, deterministic
Refcounts can't see cycles → generational cyclic GC sweeps those
Three generations, promoted on survival; can be tuned or disabled
__del__ on cycle members historically blocked collection
Freed ≠ returned to OS — arenas may retain
questions.flow: refcount frees eagerly → cycles need the generational GC → arenas may hold pages
questions.trap: "Python has a garbage collector" as the whole answer — refcounting is the main engine

questions.text: What happens on obj.attr?
points: Type's MRO searched first for a data descriptor → wins over instance dict
Then instance __dict__ → then non-data descriptors → then __getattr__ fallback
Methods are descriptors — that's how self gets bound
@property, classmethod, staticmethod, __slots__ all descriptors
MRO computed by C3 linearisation
questions.flow: data descriptor → instance dict → non-data descriptor → __getattr__
questions.trap: "instance dict is checked first" — data descriptors outrank it

questions.text: Write a decorator that times a function. What breaks if you're careless?
points: Closure over the target + *args, **kwargs passthrough
functools.wraps or you lose __name__, docstring, and annotations
Losing annotations breaks anything schema-generating downstream
Async targets need an async wrapper — one decorator can't blindly cover both
Stacking order = bottom-up application
questions.flow: closure → wraps to preserve metadata → separate async path
questions.trap: forgetting functools.wraps, then wondering why FastAPI/Pydantic misreads the signature

questions.text: Why context managers instead of try/finally?
points: __enter__ / __exit__ — cleanup travels with the resource, not the call site
__exit__ sees the exception and may suppress by returning truthy
contextlib.contextmanager for the generator form; AsyncExitStack for async
Composable: nested/stacked acquisition with correct unwind order
Right home for spans, DB sessions, temp files, model handles
questions.flow: acquire in enter → guaranteed exit → composable and reusable
questions.trap: returning truthy from __exit__ by accident and swallowing errors

questions.text: Where does Pydantic sit in a service, and what does v2 change?
points: It's the boundary — untrusted in, typed domain objects out
v2 core in Rust → large validation speedup; model_validate / model_dump
Validate once at the edge, not repeatedly in business logic
ValidationError is structured — map it to a 422, don't stringify
Same machinery emits JSON Schema → LLM tool definitions
questions.flow: untrusted edge → validate once → typed core → schema falls out for free
questions.trap: scattering model_validate through the domain layer

questions.text: gather vs TaskGroup — and what happens on cancellation?
points: Coroutine does nothing until scheduled — Task is the scheduled unit
gather(return_exceptions=False) → first error propagates, siblings keep running
TaskGroup (3.11+) → structured: one fails, rest cancelled, errors as a group
Cancellation is a CancelledError thrown in — must be allowed to propagate
Swallowing CancelledError in a bare except = ungovernable task
questions.flow: coroutine → Task → TaskGroup for structured cancel → never swallow CancelledError
questions.trap: bare except Exception that eats cancellation

questions.text: The model must return something your code can execute — how do you guarantee shape?
points: Don't parse prose — declare a schema and constrain generation
Pydantic model → JSON Schema → tool/function definition
Provider-side structured output / grammar constraining beats retry-and-hope
Still validate on receipt: schema-valid ≠ semantically valid
Failure path: repair prompt → bounded retries → fail loudly, never silently coerce
questions.flow: schema first → constrain generation → validate on arrival → bounded repair
questions.trap: regex-parsing model output, or infinite reask loops

questions.text: Someone put a blocking call in an async handler. What happens?
points: It blocks the whole event loop — every other request stalls, not just this one
Symptom: p99 collapses under load while CPU looks idle
Usual culprits: requests, sync DB driver, time.sleep, big CPU loop, file I/O
Fix: async client, or run_in_executor / asyncio.to_thread
Detect: loop.slow_callback_duration, debug mode, or latency histograms
questions.flow: one blocking call → loop stalls → all requests → offload to executor or go async
questions.trap: blaming worker count instead of naming the stalled loop

questions.text: CPU-heavy preprocessing next to your async API — where does it go?
points: Never inline in the handler — it's the blocking case with a nicer name
Small + C-backed (NumPy, tokenizer) → thread executor, GIL already released
Pure-Python heavy → process pool or a separate worker service
Truly heavy → queue + worker fleet, API returns a job handle
Deciding axis: does it hold the loop longer than your latency budget?
questions.flow: measure hold time → C-backed thread · Python-heavy process · long-running queue
questions.trap: process pool for something that pickles badly or is memory-huge

questions.text: When is __slots__ worth it?
points: Removes per-instance __dict__ → notable memory saving at high instance counts
Wins only when you have many small objects — millions of records, not a dozen services
Costs: no ad-hoc attributes, multiple-inheritance friction, weakref needs declaring
Often the wrong lever — dataclass/NamedTuple or a columnar store may beat it
Measure first; this is a profiling-led decision
questions.flow: many small instances → drop per-instance dict → verify with a memory profile
questions.trap: applying it everywhere as a style rule

questions.text: dataclass, Pydantic model, NamedTuple, or plain class?
points: dataclass — internal, trusted data; free __init__/__eq__/__repr__, no validation
Pydantic — untrusted boundary; validation + coercion + schema, real cost per object
NamedTuple — immutable, tuple-cheap, positional-friendly
Plain class — behaviour-first, invariants in methods
Rule: Pydantic at the edge, dataclass in the core
questions.flow: untrusted → Pydantic · internal → dataclass · immutable value → NamedTuple
questions.trap: Pydantic everywhere, paying validation cost on hot internal paths

questions.text: ORM or raw SQL?
points: ORM wins on CRUD, migrations, identity map, team consistency
Raw/Core wins on analytics, bulk work, window functions, tuned plans
The recurring failure is N+1 — invisible until it's in production
SQLAlchemy 2.0 lets you mix: ORM for writes, Core for read paths
Async ORM adds lazy-load hazards — eager-load explicitly
questions.flow: CRUD → ORM · analytical/bulk → Core → watch N+1 → mix deliberately
questions.trap: treating it as ideology; also lazy loading under async

questions.text: Free-threaded CPython — would you adopt it?
points: Removes the GIL → genuine multi-core Python threads
Cost: per-object locking overhead, single-thread regression, ABI churn
Blocker is the C-extension ecosystem — every native dep must support it
Honest answer: prototype yes, production only when your dep tree is green
Doesn't change I/O-bound design at all — asyncio still the answer there
questions.flow: real threads → but ecosystem gate → prototype now, adopt when deps ready
questions.trap: presenting it as free speed, or as relevant to I/O-bound work

questions.text: Sub-interpreters vs multiprocessing?
points: Per-interpreter GIL → parallelism inside one process
Cheaper than processes: no fork cost, shared memory pages, faster startup
But: no shared objects, explicit channels only; many C extensions unsupported
Fits many short CPU tasks where process spawn dominates
Still young — multiprocessing remains the boring correct answer
questions.flow: per-interpreter GIL → in-process parallelism → cheap spawn, but isolation and ext gaps
questions.trap: describing them as threads with shared state

questions.text: Where do you put the cache, and what does it cost you?
points: Layers: in-process (lru_cache) · shared (Redis) · CDN/edge
In-process is fastest and wrong the moment you scale horizontally — N caches, N truths
Shared cache = network hop + a new failure mode + serialisation cost
Invalidation strategy chosen before the cache: TTL · write-through · versioned key
For LLM work the interesting ones are embedding and semantic caches
questions.flow: pick layer → accept its consistency story → decide invalidation up front
questions.trap: lru_cache on a multi-worker service and calling it a cache hit rate

questions.text: Make this endpoint idempotent.
points: Client sends an idempotency key; server stores key → result
Same key again → replay the stored response, don't re-execute
Key must be persisted in the same transaction as the effect, or you get double-writes
Need a state machine: in-flight vs done — concurrent duplicates must block, not race
TTL the keys; decide what a conflicting body on the same key means (409)
questions.flow: key in → atomic claim → execute once → store result → replay on repeat
questions.trap: storing the key after the side effect — the crash window is exactly the bug

questions.text: Which rate-limiting algorithm, and why?
points: Fixed window — trivial, but boundary burst gives 2× at the edge
Sliding window — smoother, more state
Token bucket — allows controlled burst, the usual right answer for APIs
Leaky bucket — smooths output, good in front of a fragile upstream
Distributed → shared counter in Redis, atomic Lua; decide fail-open vs fail-closed
questions.flow: burst tolerance? → token bucket → shared atomic counter → pick fail mode
questions.trap: per-process limiters that multiply your real limit by worker count

questions.text: You fan out to five providers and two fail. How do you surface that?
points: TaskGroup + ExceptionGroup — all failures, not just the first
except* matches by type inside the group
Preserves partial success — critical for multi-source retrieval and tool fan-out
Decide the policy explicitly: all-or-nothing vs best-effort-with-report
Log the group; don't collapse to one error string
questions.flow: TaskGroup → ExceptionGroup → except* → explicit partial-failure policy
questions.trap: gather + first-exception, silently losing the other four outcomes

questions.text: Protocol or ABC?
points: ABC = nominal — you must inherit; explicit, discoverable, runtime-enforced
Protocol = structural — shape is enough, no inheritance, no coupling
Protocol shines for third-party or swappable types you don't own
@runtime_checkable only checks method presence, not signatures
Practical: Protocol for ports/adapters, ABC when you're also sharing implementation
questions.flow: do I own the type? → no → Protocol · sharing behaviour too → ABC
questions.trap: trusting runtime_checkable as real validation

questions.text: Memory climbs until the pod OOMs every couple of days. Find it.
points: Separate the three: leak (refs retained) · fragmentation (arenas) · legit growth (cache with no bound)
tracemalloc snapshots + diff between two points under load
gc.get_objects() / referrer chains for what's holding the graph
Usual suspects: unbounded cache/dict, module-level accumulator, closure capturing a big object, un-awaited tasks
RSS not falling after free ≠ leak — allocator may retain
questions.flow: snapshot → diff under load → find retainer → classify leak vs fragmentation vs unbounded cache
questions.trap: reading RSS alone and concluding "leak"

questions.text: How many workers and threads for this service?
points: ASGI: one event loop per worker process; workers ≈ cores for CPU headroom
Async I/O-bound → few workers, high concurrency each
Sync framework/handlers → thread pool sizing dominates, not worker count
Memory is the real ceiling when each worker loads a model — workers × model size
Preload/fork to share read-only pages where the runtime allows
questions.flow: workers ≈ cores → concurrency inside the loop → but memory per worker caps it
questions.trap: scaling workers for an async service that's actually blocked on one call

questions.text: Connection pool under async load — what goes wrong?
points: Pool is per process, so real DB load = pool × workers × replicas
Async lets you accept far more concurrency than the pool can serve → queueing at checkout
Symptom: latency climbs with no DB CPU movement — it's pool wait, not query time
Always set acquire timeout; unbounded wait turns into a hang
Long transactions hold connections — keep the transaction narrower than the request
questions.flow: pool per process → concurrency exceeds it → checkout queue → cap and time out
questions.trap: growing the pool instead of shortening transaction hold time

questions.text: Stream tokens to the browser. What actually bites?
points: SSE for one-way token streams; WebSocket only if you need duplex
Disable proxy buffering or nothing appears until the end (nginx X-Accel-Buffering)
Backpressure: slow client → your generator must not race ahead unbounded
Client disconnect must cancel upstream or you pay for tokens nobody reads
Errors mid-stream: headers already sent → in-band error event, not a 500
questions.flow: SSE → unbuffer proxy → honour backpressure → cancel on disconnect → in-band errors
questions.trap: assuming disconnect stops the upstream LLM call

questions.text: It's slow. What do you reach for?
points: Measure before guessing — wall-clock first, then decide CPU vs wait
Deterministic (cProfile) for call counts; sampling (py-spy) for live prod, no restart
py-spy dump on a hung process shows where it's actually parked
Async needs task-aware views — a stalled loop shows as idle CPU
Optimise the top of the profile, then re-measure; stop when the budget is met
questions.flow: wall-clock → sample in prod → find the hot frame → fix → re-measure
questions.trap: micro-optimising a function that isn't in the top of the profile

questions.text: When does work move to a queue, and what breaks there?
points: Move when: longer than the request budget · retryable · spiky · needs isolation
Delivery is at-least-once → consumers must be idempotent (see #24)
Poison messages need a DLQ and a bounded retry with backoff
Visibility timeout must exceed real processing time or you get duplicate work
Ordering is not free — per-key partitioning if you need it
questions.flow: exceeds budget → enqueue → idempotent consumer → bounded retry → DLQ
questions.trap: assuming exactly-once

questions.text: One request spans five services. How do you trace it?
points: Correlation/trace ID generated at the edge, propagated on every hop
contextvars carries it across await boundaries — thread-locals do not
Structured logs (JSON) with the ID as a field, not baked into the message
OpenTelemetry spans give causality and timing, not just breadcrumbs
Propagate into background tasks explicitly — context does not follow a fire-and-forget task for free
questions.flow: ID at edge → contextvars → structured field → spans → propagate into workers
questions.trap: thread-locals under asyncio; losing context in background tasks

questions.text: Design the Python service in front of an LLM.
points: Edge: validate (Pydantic) → authn/z → rate limit per tenant → idempotency key
Async all the way to the provider; stream back via SSE
Reliability: timeout · bounded retry with jitter · circuit breaker · fallback model
Cost controls: token budget per request, semantic cache, truncate context deliberately
Observability: tokens in/out, cost, TTFT, p99, cache-hit — per tenant
questions.flow: validate → limit → async call → stream → breaker + budget → per-tenant metrics
questions.trap: designing it like a CRUD API — no TTFT, no token budget, no breaker

questions.text: Same service also does embedding and reranking. Now what?
points: Two different workload shapes in one process = the core mistake
Split: async API tier ‖ CPU/GPU worker tier, queue between them
Batch embeddings — per-item calls waste both GPU and network
Model load is memory × workers; load once, share, or isolate the tier entirely
Backpressure at the queue, not by dropping HTTP requests
questions.flow: separate the tiers → queue between → batch on the worker → bound the queue
questions.trap: one process doing both, then tuning workers forever

questions.text: Dependency management across a team — what's your policy?
points: Lockfile committed; the resolver output is the artifact, not the range
Separate direct deps from transitive — pin apps, range libraries
One environment per project; reproducible build in CI from the lock
The AI stack is the hard part: torch/CUDA pins, extras, platform wheels
Upgrade cadence + a CVE path, or the lock quietly rots
questions.flow: declare ranges → resolve → commit lock → CI builds from lock → scheduled upgrades
questions.trap: pip freeze as a lockfile — it can't tell direct from transitive

questions.text: What do you instrument in an AI backend that you wouldn't in a CRUD one?
points: TTFT and inter-token latency — averages hide the experience
Tokens in/out and cost per request, attributed per tenant/feature
Retrieval quality signals: hit rate, rerank movement, empty-result rate
Model/prompt version on every span — otherwise regressions aren't attributable
Guardrail and refusal counts as first-class metrics
questions.flow: latency shape (TTFT) → cost per tenant → retrieval signals → version tag everything
questions.trap: p99 latency and error rate only — invisible to quality and cost regressions

questions.text: When do you drop to C/Rust?
points: Only after profiling says a tight Python loop is the bottleneck
First try: vectorise (NumPy), better algorithm, or an existing native lib
Real candidates: custom tokenisation, bespoke distance metrics, hot parsers
Costs: build matrix, wheels per platform, debugging across the boundary, hiring
Boundary crossing itself costs — batch across it, don't call per item
questions.flow: profile → vectorise/algorithm first → native only for a proven hot loop → batch the boundary
questions.trap: rewriting in Rust something that was one bad query all along

questions.text: Tell me about a Python performance or concurrency problem you actually fixed.
points: Symptom in user terms first — latency, cost, or an outage — never "the code was slow"
What you thought it was, and the measurement that proved you wrong
The tool that found it — name it (py-spy, tracemalloc, trace view)
The fix and what you deliberately didn't do
The number: before → after. This is the sentence they remember
questions.flow: user-visible symptom → wrong hypothesis → measurement → fix → number
questions.trap: narrating the fix with no before/after figure

questions.text: (D) "Your multiprocessing code works on Linux, breaks on Mac. Why?
points: Linux fork — child inherits memory copy-on-write, no pickling
macOS (3.8+) and Windows spawn — fresh interpreter, re-imports the module
So spawn needs picklable args and the if __name__ == "__main__": guard
Fork + threads is genuinely unsafe — locks can be inherited held
Loaded ML models: fork shares pages cheaply, spawn reloads per worker
questions.flow: fork inherits vs spawn re-imports → picklable args + main guard → memory story differs
questions.trap: assuming worker startup cost and memory are the same on both

questions.text: (C) "Why is pickle dangerous, and what do you use instead?
points: Unpickling executes arbitrary code — it's deserialisation and code execution
Never unpickle anything crossing a trust boundary: uploads, cache, queue payloads
Untrusted → JSON / msgpack / protobuf, or model_dump_json()
Trusted internal (sklearn artifacts) is defensible with version pinning + integrity check
Also brittle: pickles break across library versions
questions.flow: unpickle = code execution → never across trust boundary → JSON/msgpack out, pinned artifacts in
questions.trap: treating it as "just a serialisation format choice"

questions.text: (C) "@cached_property, @lru_cache, functools.cache — which and when?
points: cached_property — per instance, computed once, lives in __dict__; dies with the object
lru_cache(maxsize) — per function, keyed on args, bounded eviction
cache — unbounded lru_cache; on a method it pins self forever → leak
Args must be hashable; mutable defaults and unhashable payloads break it
All are per-process — see #23 before calling it a cache layer
questions.flow: instance-scoped → cached_property · arg-keyed bounded → lru_cache · unbounded on methods → leak
questions.trap: @cache on an instance method, then hunting a memory leak

questions.text: (C) "CPython, PyPy, or compiled Python?
points: CPython — reference, best C-extension compatibility; the default for AI stacks
PyPy — tracing JIT, big wins on long-running pure-Python; weak native-ext story
mypyc / Cython — AOT-compile typed modules, ship as extensions
3.11+ specialising interpreter narrowed the gap for a lot of workloads
For AI work the dep tree usually decides it — torch/CUDA pins you to CPython
questions.flow: pure-Python hot loop → PyPy/mypyc · native deps → CPython → the dep tree usually decides
questions.trap: proposing PyPy for a torch service
